I bought this several years ago and have used it several times a day every day since. It is very fast, much faster than gas.There is a learning curve on heat. The default setting is 5 which is too high for anything other than searing meat.  I find that even 3 is too high for general cooking, and used 2 for is better.  True it does have a "hot spot" in the middle on high  heat but I simply work around it.I leave stock and such at 1 and get a nice low simmer in a covered pot. One thing you can not do is move the pan around a lot, the unit beeps and if you persist, such as the continuous shaking of a kettle while popping corn you will ruin the unit. A friend proved that very nicely. I would recommend this highly to anyone interested in  induction cooking.

I've never had a cast-iron skillet get so hot so fast. On power 2 it fries nicely. On power 10 it boils water much faster than my gas range. It makes it's own kind of noise - not bad, just noticeable, like a big transformer sound - and a fan comes on inside of it to keep the guts cool. The fan keeps running when its turned off for a while, until it cools down. But the top only gets hot from the vessel, not from the cooker, so anything that spills over is easy to wipe up - nothing gets burned on.

Update - 6 months in... Okay, the weather has warmed up and I've been using it more. I have discovered to be true what I saw mentioned in another review. There are two circles marked on the surface, implying to me the active areas of induction. But when i use a pan the size of the biggest circle, only the smaller circle area heats. So with a small cast iron pan (6"), the whole thing heats great. But with a 10" pan, the center gets hot, and not the rest. I don't know if this is something intrinsic about induction physics, or if there just aren't the guts underneath to actually work the larger circle area. Either way, I have to accommodate that by turning things around to get them into the hot center. This causes me to knock two stars off. It's that big a deal. On my gas top at least the whole thing gets hot, even if it's not as hot, as fast. This is obvious and measurable, just with a little oil in the pan, you can see exactly where the heat is, and
Best toy I ever got! This thing boils water at warp speeds! Great for cooking sugar!

This cooker is build like many others. They are made in china and are made from the same blueprint, 10 levels of power and temp with a timer.

There are some loose ends that in my opinion need to be addressed. Those things to correct are the following:

1. When you use the timer, the led of timer goes off when returns to Temp or Power instead of remaining it on, so you have the information that the timer is activated together with the function light of Power or Temp;
2. 10 levels of temperature is just too little, jumping 20 degrees is to much to allow better tuning, 10 degrees is the maximum acceptable;
3. Heating by temperature setting always assumes maximum power, something that might burn the ingredients, like milk. The temperature adjustment should assume the power defined previously before switching, to be able to achieve a temperature through a preferred power.

To solve all the previous points, it will be more intuitive if the functions were cumulative, Power and Temperature and/or Time. Given a Power, it should be possible to restrict by Temperature and Timer, where the value 0 means no restriction, and so, no light informing the existing restriction! The Power light means it's on while the others ones mean the respective restriction, temperature and time function, ideally with an unitary adjustment in degrees and minutes. To know that Temperature or Time is being adjusted, the respective light would flash, no flashing always m

I purchased this because I wanted the (Forum Recommended) 1800 Watts of power. I find the 10 temperature setting to be fine for my needs. Something about the Max Burton that I really like is the ability to remove the cooking vessel from the surface without having it shutdown. There are a lot of times I remove a pan from the cooking surface to flip, tip, drain, etc. The Max Burton beeps letting you know the pan is missing but you do have a few seconds to replace the pan before the unit shut down. Along with the cooktop I also ordered a new set of T-fal Nonstick Cookware that is induction capable. My old pots and pans had seen better days.

I strongly recommend the Max Burton 6200. It's fast, safe, and easy to clean. I must say it also look very nice sitting on my counter. Last weak I was making french onion soup and needed to go to the grocery store for some beef stock. I never left the house with a gas range burner lit but walking away from the 6200 is like walking away from a crock pot. I covered the pan, turned the temp down and ran my errand.

This unit was a huge disappointment, and I returned it for a SPT1300. 210 doesn't boil water after a few minutes, the clock beeps only sometimes. I bought it for the stainless steel, but it's not worth it. I had aan SPT1300 which worked like a charm for a few years, 5-6 times/day, kept accurate heat. The Burton will boil water at 210 for a few minutes, then not, and 250 is too high. The temps on the SPT were 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 190, 210, 230, and so on, with an eight hour timer, just what I need for bone broth.
I've had 2 of them for the last 5 years, no problems at all.  At full power these are consuming 1800 watts they will fail if they have to run in brownout conditions.
BE SURE TO TEST YOUR POTS/PANS WITH A MAGNET BEFORE YOU BUY IT.

Wish I had bought this sooner, it's great! I used this for the first time today to make pasta. I have a new 5 burner gas range and it has been taking about 30' to get a big pot of water boiling for pasta. Today I used a large Le Creuset dutch oven on my new Max Burton Induction cook top and my water was boiling in around 10 to 12' and my pasta was cooked in a total of 22' from start to finish. This was amazing to me, because I was using a heavy cast iron pan with about 5 quarts of water. I used the #10 setting to get the water boiling and then turned it down to #8 setting to finish cooking. I stirred the pot several times during cooking say 5 or 6 times and my pasta was perfect. It was simple to use and the instructions are written in easy to understand English and French. Clean up of the cook top was easy, it wiped clean with a wet dish cloth, ( there was a little condensation from the rapid boiling).

Most of my cookware will not work on this cook top, but I don't see that as a problem. I have a few pieces of nice cast iron and just purchased a couple of All-Clad pieces, a 6 quart pot and 12" skillet. I can't see needing any more pieces other than maybe a small sauce pot. I cook for 4 to 7 people, depending on who is at home at dinner time.

When I first got it I was sold. Since I don't have a stove top in my place, the 6200 was a game changer. I could sear a steak. Quick fry. Rapidly boil water. Heats fast (without heating my kitchen in the summer time). Far more fire safe than a coiled counter top burner.

And it broke. I heard other induction coolers had a limited life span, but this one was of the better models. Its kaput less than two years into owning it. First it would sporadically not start at all. Then the internal cooling fan became completely non-responsive.

The 6200 would be a five star item if it lasted longer. I'm used to replacing $20 coiled burners once a year. But this item's too expensive to be of the throw-away variety.

Here's my delima... do I buy the cheapest induction cooker with the understanding the aren't expected to last, or go the other route and get the nicest one I can find?
I especially enjoy the safety features.

Don't know if it is any better than the BergHoff I already had, just better priced and wondering if I should have paid the higher. Nothing wrong with it except the controls are not as good as Berghoff...

Berghoff > capacitance
Max Burton > membrane

Berghoff > time in 5 min first press
Max Burton > time in 1 min first press

Berghoff > very easy to tell what the single display is displaying
Max Burton > NOT easy to tell what the single display is displaying > at times two indicator lights on at once like power and time can't tell which it is... and manual says nothing about it.

Berghoff > Fan does not cool down when shutting off
Max Burton > Fan does cool down when shutting off

Overall except for controls I think they are all similar and are stamped out by the SAME Chinese manufacture, just branded different.

I bought this to test out what induction cooking is like as we were considering buying an in-counter cooktop. I love the idea of induction cooking—I remember as a kid (when induction was crazy expensive) I thought it was so Star Trek that I could barely wait the 30 years it would take for me to be in a position to buy a stovetop. And better yet, it doesn't produce the excess heat waste that any other power source does, so it is greener *and* more pleasant to use. (Gas and electric pump waste heat out pretty bad, and to double the inefficiency, that generally means you air conditioner will be doing extra duty.)

The promise of precision cooking and near-immediate temperature changes is really exciting, but this model absolutely doesn't live up. I've tested with laser thermometers and plain boil tests in a variety of good pans, and this one has bad hot-spots and cold spots; adjusting the temperature doesn't take effect quickly, even if you change it by a lot; and anything above 3 or 4 (on a scale of TEN) is way too hot for most anything except nuking a pot of water.

I DO UNDERSTAND that an inexpensive tabletop model could never be a very accurate example of what cooking on a "real" Bertazzoni or Wolf or GE cooktop or range would be like. Nevertheless, I was hoping this would be good enough to give us the confidence of buying an expensive induction cooktop, and it did the opposite.

The fan seems much quieter in this model, and of course this has the stainless steel finish which my older model did not. It looks good and works just like the old one.

For folks not familiar with the max burton induction, it has 10 power level settings where level 1 and 2 are just cycling the power on and off at different rates (more time on at 2, less time on at 1), and then power levels 3 and above are all continuously on and provide increasing power levels up to the 10 setting which is 1800 watts. We use this every day for boiling tea water in a kettle because it is fast, and use it for other cooking as well. For the price, this is a great model.

The disadvantage of this relatively cheap model is that you find when cooking that you would like to have about 10 different settings between zero (below the "1" setting) and the "3" setting. But it is fantastic for boiling water and for cooking that does not require fine-tuning a low heat setting.

This number let him know that I had received an old unit, one manufactured in 2010 and one that had probably been refurbished given that the unit look as though it had been used as there is a scratch on the unit. He stated that I should have received a new unit manufactured in 2017 and that I should return the product.  So, I am in the process of returning the product which would be easier if I had a printer - but I don't,  I'm paperless!  So, there's that. Best one I've tried yet.  It's easy to remove the filter with a push from the bottom spring mechanism.  You don't have to touch the filter and risk it tearing and spilling the grinds.  The only problem is that over time, the lid starts pushing up and opens sometimes causing the grinds to spill and make a mess.  To avoid this, you have to be careful not to overfill the grinds and leave room for the compression from the spring mechanism.  To much pressure from overfilling and the lid pops up.  You do this trick, and life is good.
Don't waste your money. Coffee grinds constantly get into the coffee cup and it's like drinking slightly flavored hot water.

We've been using this filter for nearly a year now and it works great.  Cleanup is easy...we use our own special coffee from Guatemala...and it's a lot less expensive than the K-Cups.  We love them.  I prepare them the night before, so we just pop them into our Keurig 2.0 and brew in the mornings.  We've only had one problem...which was my fault.  We left one of the cups in the brewer overnight and it dried out and stuck to the cup.  When I removed it...which wasn't difficult.  the little silicon sealing ring (on the lid) came off.  I didn't see it and apparently threw it away with the used bag.  I now am more careful and have no problems.  We just ordered our third round of filters from Amazon...1000 of them...so we plan to brew with this system for a long time...

goodbye,  stale coffee grounds that have been stored in plastic cups "forever" and are not biodegradable or eco-friendly.  I can freshly grind my own beans every day! ..offer variety. Reduce storage of boxes of pods. A great product!
